372.title: Intention is the act
372.hook: the Buddha calls intention itself kamma (AN 6.63)
372.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often explain kamma by pointing to intention, and many practitioners make a habit of checking their motive before acting and of dedicating good deeds with a wholesome wish.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma kammanta, right action, a way of moving through the world with care. Your line: act with care.

Two people step on your foot on the same crowded train. One lurches when the brakes hit. The other looks right at you first, and then does it. Same foot. Same weight. Same bruise. And yet nobody would call them the same event. No philosophy class required; a small child on a playground already argues the difference between an accident and on purpose. The Buddha built a teaching on that instinct, and he put it in a single short sentence.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, ONE FOOT.` → `A LURCH, OR A LOOK FIRST.` → `SAME BRUISE, DIFFERENT EVENT.`

segments.voice: The sentence is in the Numbered Discourses, in a sutta about seeing deeply into the teaching. The Buddha says, in plain terms: it is intention, monks, that I call kamma. Having intended, a person acts by body, by speech, and by mind. The Pali word for intention is cetanā: the mind's leaning toward something, its choosing. And kamma, karma in Sanskrit, simply means action, deed. Not fate. Not a cosmic scoreboard. A deed. So this is a definition, and a startling one. Which part of the train was the deed? Not the foot. The choosing. That's why the path spent days on right intention before it reached speech and action. The hand and the tongue are where an act shows up; the mind is where it's made. Two things follow. First, accidents aren't the heart of kamma. The lurch on the train isn't what the Buddha is pointing at, though carelessness can be a kind of choice too. Second, and harder: a deed can be done entirely inside. A long, deliberate grudge is a deed, even if no one ever sees it. The Dhammapada opens with the same idea, in Max Müller's words: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." So if intention is the act, the place to practice is the half-second before the act. That small gap is where the choosing lives, and the choosing is the part that's yours.

segments.voice: Rest with the breath and watch for the choosing: small impulses will arrive, to shift your weight, to scratch, to open your eyes, to check the time. Before you act on one, see whether you can catch the intention itself, the little lean toward doing. You may act on it or not; the point is to see it before the body moves.
Kamma. Action, deed; karma in Sanskrit. The Buddha defines it by intention, cetanā: having intended, one acts.
Your line: the half-second before the act. The hand is where it shows; the mind is where it's made. Catch you tomorrow.

373.title: As you sow
373.hook: as the seed is sown, so is the fruit reaped (SN 11.10)
373.howItsDone: Buddhists often speak of good deeds as planting seeds of merit, and many make small daily offerings or acts of generosity with that image in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kamma, a deed, made in the mind by intention. Your line: the half-second before the act.

Long ago, the Buddha says, a group of gentle seers lived in leaf huts by the sea. War was coming, the gods on one side and the asuras, the titans, on the other, and the seers were afraid the titans would harm them. So they went to the titans' king, a fearsome lord named Sambara, and asked him for one thing: a promise of safety. He laughed at them. No safety for you, he said. I give you fear instead. What the seers said back is a picture any farmer knows.
screen: `LEAF HUTS BY THE SEA.` → `A PROMISE OF SAFETY, PLEASE.` → `NO. I GIVE YOU FEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's their answer, close to the Pali. You give us fear when we ask for safety. Then let fear be yours, without end. As the seed that's sown, so is the fruit that's reaped. The one who does good reaps good; the one who does evil reaps evil. You've planted this seed, friend; you'll taste its fruit. Then the seers vanish. And that night, the sutta says, Sambara wakes in terror three times. Two things in this strange little story are worth noticing. First, the seers do wish him endless fear, but they don't lift a hand to bring it. They point to something they trust is already true: a seed grows into its own kind of plant. Plant fear, and fear is what comes up. Nobody has to deliver it. Second, the fruit can begin sooner than you'd think. Sambara doesn't wait a lifetime. The same night, the fear he handed out is in his own bed. That's the farmer's view of kamma. Yesterday said the deed is the intention. Today says the intention is a seed. Seeds don't sprout on demand; some come up in a season, some take years, and the suttas say kamma can ripen in this life or later ones. But no farmer plants chilies and expects to pull up melons. Pali talks about kamma's phala, its fruit, and its vipāka, its ripening: the language of an orchard.

segments.voice: Picture today as a field you've been walking through, scattering seeds without looking: a sharp reply, a kind note, an hour of scrolling, a promise kept. 374.title: Not everything is kamma
374.hook: asked whether all feeling comes from past deeds, the Buddha says no: weather, illness and more play a part (SN 36.21)
374.howItsDone: Buddhist communities visit and care for the sick, and monks are traditionally invited to chant protective verses for the ill; teachers often cite this sutta to correct the idea that illness is simply a punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: phala, fruit, and the seers' seed that grows its own kind. Your line: chilies don't grow into melons.

Someone you love gets sick. And sooner or later, someone says it, kindly or not: it must be their karma. Maybe something from a past life. Sometimes the sick person says it about themselves, lying awake at three in the morning: what did I do to deserve this? The idea gets pinned on Buddhism. The Buddha was asked about it directly, by a wandering ascetic named Sivaka, and his answer isn't the one the question expects.
screen: `IT MUST BE THEIR KARMA.` → `WHAT DID I DO TO DESERVE THIS?` → `SIVAKA ASKS.`

segments.voice: Sivaka puts it plainly. Some teachers say that whatever a person feels, pleasant, painful or neither, is all caused by what they did in the past. What do you say? The Buddha says no, and gives a list. Some feelings, Sivaka, arise from bile. Some from phlegm. Some from wind, which in the medicine of his day meant the body's inner airs. Some from a mix of these. Some from a change of season, the weather. Some from careless behavior, how a person treats their own body. Some from assault, what someone else does to you. And some from the ripening of kamma. Eight causes. Kamma is one of them. Then he says something sharp about the teachers who claim it's all past deeds: they go beyond what a person can know for themselves, and beyond what the world agrees is true. Anyone can see that a cold snap brings on aches. So kamma is real in this teaching, and it isn't the whole explanation. Later Buddhist thinkers worked out in detail how kamma and other conditions weave together, and they don't all draw the lines in the same place. But the sutta's practical point is hard to miss. By this text, telling a sick person their illness is simply their own past doing claims to know what no one in the room can know. The response that fits the sutta is the one a good doctor and a good friend would give anyway: let's look after you.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is unwell or struggling right now; it may be you. If a blaming thought is hiding in the picture, they should have, I should have, it's because, don't argue with it; set it gently to one side, the way you'd move a coat off a chair so someone can sit down. Then let what's left be simple care, the plain wish that they're looked after, and rest there with the breath.
Vedana, feeling. In the Connected Discourses the Buddha names eight causes of feeling, from bile to weather to assault, and kamma is only one.
Your line: let's look after you. Kamma is real here, and it isn't the whole story. Take good care.

375.title: The acrobats
375.hook: protecting yourself you protect others; protecting others you protect yourself (SN 47.19)
375.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the acrobat story to show that personal practice and care for others aren't in competition; many practitioners pair daily mindfulness with acts of patience and kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vedana, feeling, with eight causes and kamma only one. Your line: let's look after you.

Long ago, the Buddha tells his monks, an acrobat sets up a tall bamboo pole and calls to his apprentice, Medakathalika: climb the pole and stand on my shoulders. She does. Then he says the sensible-sounding thing. You look after me, and I'll look after you. That way we'll show our skill, collect our fee, and get down safely. And from up on his shoulders, she says no. The Buddha is staying near a town called Sedaka when he tells this story, and he takes her side.
screen: `A BAMBOO POLE.` → `YOU WATCH ME, I'LL WATCH YOU.` → `FROM HIS SHOULDERS: NO.`

segments.voice: Here's her answer. That's not the way, master. You protect yourself, and I'll protect myself. Guarded and protected like that, we'll show our skill, collect our fee, and come down safely. And the Buddha says: that's the method. It sounds backward at first. Isn't looking after each other the kind thing? But picture it. She's high up on his shoulders, trying to watch his feet. He's balancing a pole while trying to watch her. Both of them are looking at the wrong thing. If each keeps their own balance, the whole act holds. Then the Buddha turns the picture into a teaching with two sides. Protecting yourself, you protect others. How? By practicing mindfulness, developing it, making much of it. A steady person is safer to be around. Protecting others, you protect yourself. How? By patience, by harmlessness, by loving-kindness, by care. A kind person lives with fewer enemies. So it isn't selfish against selfless. It's one movement, seen from two directions. That's why this sits beside right action. Someone off balance can't hold anyone up for long, and someone who harms others is never really safe. Consider the person in a family or an office everyone leans on. The best thing they can give the people on their shoulders may be their own steadiness.

segments.voice: Stand up if you can, or sit tall, and feel your feet or your seat carrying your weight; find your own balance, not rigid, just centered. Then think of one person who leans on you, and notice that your steadiness, right now, is already part of how you hold them. Come back to your own center, and rest there.
The acrobats. Protecting yourself through mindfulness protects others; protecting others through patience and kindness protects you.
Your line: the acrobat's balance. Guarding yourself guards others, and guarding others guards you. Day three hundred seventy-five, and steady.

376.title: Five great gifts
376.hook: keeping the precepts gives countless beings freedom from fear (AN 8.39)
376.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists commonly take the three refuges and the five precepts together, often chanting them in Pali after a monk at the temple or at home; some teachers frame the precepts as gifts of safety to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the acrobats, each keeping their own balance so the whole act holds. Your line: the acrobat's balance.

A neighbor who has never once lied to you. A coworker who would never take what's yours. A friend who stays clear-headed at the party and drives everyone home. None of them hands you anything. Around people like that, nothing happens, and the nothing is the point: there's no harm coming. It's easy to miss, because it never makes a sound. The Buddha had a name for what they give. He called it a gift. Five of them, in fact.
screen: `NEVER LIED, NEVER TOOK.` → `NOTHING HAPPENS.` → `IT WAS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: The sutta is in the Numbered Discourses, in the book of eights, and it's about streams of merit: eight ways goodness keeps flowing. The first three are going for refuge, to the Buddha, the teaching and the community. The last five are the five precepts. But here the Buddha doesn't call them rules. He calls them gifts, great gifts, and adds a long row of praise: ancient, traditional, pure, never scorned by the wise. Here's how the first one works. When someone gives up killing, the Buddha says, they give countless beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from oppression. And by giving that, they receive the same: a share in that freedom without measure. He says the same of not stealing, of no sexual misconduct, of not lying, and of not taking intoxicants that cloud the mind. Notice the word countless. A gift of money reaches one person. This gift reaches everyone who crosses your path, and many who never will: the stranger whose wallet you hand back, the animal in your yard. They don't have to know about it. And the giver gets the same gift back: a life without the fear of being found out, without enemies made by your own hands. The Pali for freedom from fear is abhaya, and Buddhist teachers speak of giving it, abhaya-dāna, as a form of generosity in its own right. It costs nothing, and it doesn't run out.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people and creatures you'll cross paths with today, at home, on the street, at work, the dog next door, the spider in the corner, and picture each one, just for a moment, safe from you. Not because you've decided to be nice, but because, with you, there's simply nothing to fear. Let that safety spread wider than you can picture, and notice how it feels in your own body to be that kind of person.
Abhaya, freedom from fear. In the book of eights, the five precepts are gifts: freedom from fear given to countless beings, and returned to the giver.

377.title: Right livelihood
377.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists reflect on whether their work causes harm, and some choose or change careers with right livelihood in mind; monastics live on what is freely offered and are not to earn by fortune telling or by flattering donors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abhaya, freedom from fear, and the five precepts as great gifts. Your line: a gift to everyone.

Ask anyone at a party what they do, and they'll tell you their job. Not their hobbies, not their values: their job. Work fills a large share of a waking week. So it's striking that, of the eight factors on the Buddha's path, one is entirely about how you earn your living. Not whether you meditate on your lunch break. Not a prayer before the commute. The work itself, and what it does to people.
screen: `SO, WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `A LARGE SHARE OF THE WEEK.` → `ONE FACTOR FOR THE WORK ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Sammā ājīva. Ājīva means livelihood, the way a person keeps themselves alive, from jīva, life. In the great forty sutta, the definition is short: a noble disciple gives up wrong livelihood and makes a living by right livelihood. For the details, the canon looks in two directions. For monks and nuns, wrong livelihood has a surprising list. The first sutta of the Long Discourses names what it calls low arts: reading palms, interpreting dreams, predicting eclipses, picking lucky days, casting charms. The Buddha's monks weren't to live by any of them. And the great forty sutta names quieter wrongs: scheming, flattering, dropping hints for donations, belittling others to get gifts, and using one gift to fish for a bigger one. Fortune telling and sweet talk, it turns out, were how a holy person could make a living dishonestly. For lay people, the test is simpler: earn your living honestly, by your own effort, without harming. Tomorrow's sutta names specific trades to avoid. Right livelihood sits beside right speech and right action for a reason: it's speech and action done all day, every working day, for pay. A job can quietly ask you to shade the truth to a customer, cut a corner no one will see, or push people toward what they don't need. The path doesn't say quit your job. It says look at your work as honestly as you'd look at your words.

segments.voice: Bring your work to mind, whatever it is, a job, caring for a family, studying, looking for work, and picture an ordinary hour of it. Ask first, without accusing yourself, where this work helps, and let that be clear. Then, gently, ask whether it anywhere asks you to shade the truth or harm someone a little, and just notice, with no verdicts today.
Sammā ājīva. Right livelihood: earning a living honestly and without harm. The fifth factor of the path.
Your line: earn clean. It's speech and action, done all day, for pay. That's day three hundred seventy-seven.

378.title: Five trades
378.hook: lay followers avoid trading in weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants and poisons (AN 5.177)
378.howItsDone: Many lay Buddhists avoid work in the five trades, and some extend the principle to how they invest and spend; teachers often cite this sutta when discussing right livelihood.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma ajiva, right livelihood, earning a living honestly and without harm. Your line: earn clean. Today ends the week.

Your money is busy right now, while you're sitting here. The coffee you bought this morning, the bank holding your paycheck, the retirement fund you haven't looked at since the day you signed up. Each one is quietly paying for something, somewhere, and most of us have no idea what. The Buddha's world had no index funds. But it had markets, caravans and merchants, and he named five things a lay follower shouldn't trade in.
screen: `YOUR MONEY IS BUSY.` → `COFFEE, BANK, RETIREMENT FUND.` → `PAYING FOR SOMETHING, SOMEWHERE.`

segments.voice: In the Numbered Discourses, the sutta is only a few lines long. A lay follower, the Buddha says, should not engage in five kinds of trade: trade in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants, and in poisons. That's nearly the whole text. The old commentary fills in some meaning. Living beings, it says, means people: buying and selling human beings. Meat means raising and selling animals for slaughter. All five share a shape: the goods themselves are made to harm, to kill, to enslave, or to cloud the mind. Notice who it's addressed to. Not monks; they don't trade at all. This is for householders with shops and caravans. It doesn't say commerce is wrong. Elsewhere the Buddha describes a shopkeeper who is shrewd, capable and trustworthy, and says he soon grows rich. It draws a line around five kinds of goods. It also doesn't settle whether to eat meat; Buddhist communities differ on that, and this sutta is about the trade. Buddhists today read it in different ways. Some read it narrowly, as a list of businesses to stay out of. Others widen it into a question about everything their money touches: what their savings fund, what their spending supports. The sutta itself doesn't say how wide to read it. But the question it plants is plain: what does your money do when you're not watching? Look back at the week. Intention is the act. As you sow. Not everything is kamma. The acrobat's balance. A gift to everyone. Earn clean. And today, what your money does.
screen: `FIVE LINES, FIVE TRADES.` · `GOODS MADE TO HARM.` · `FOR HOUSEHOLDERS, NOT MONKS.` · `HOW WIDE TO READ IT.` · then, large: `WHAT YOUR MONEY DOES.`

segments.voice: Think of the last three things you paid for, and follow each one back a step: who made it, who sold it, where the money went next. You won't know everything, and that's fine; just notice the trail, and how rarely anyone looks at it. Then rest with the breath, and let a quiet question sit there: what would I want my money to do?
Five trades. Weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants and poisons: the five a lay follower doesn't trade in, from the book of fives.
Your line: what your money does. The sutta leaves it to you how wide to read it. That's the week.

chat.says: Does Buddhism say business or getting rich is wrong?

Yes; a lay follower should avoid all trade and commerce of any kind.
